notes: Ruling slot 1 is the PDCS, governing since 1957 with the PSDIS (joint 'Popular Alliance', 38 of 60 seats in 1969); Captains Regent Ghironzi (PDCS) and Casali (PSDIS founder). The real partner PSDIS is social democratic and sits in slot 3; the template coalition slot 2 holds the liberal MLS (1 seat). The PSS goes to slot 18 (non-aligned left socialism, with its own MD sprite) instead of MD's slot 19, which holds the Maoist CP(ML) that contested 1969. The Church (Diocese of Montefeltro) follows MD in slot 23.

0.name: Gli Uomini di Rovereta
0.text:
The Men of Rovereta are the hard core of the anti-communist bloc forged in the autumn of 1957, when defectors from the left gave the opposition a majority and its councillors set up a provisional government in a factory at Rovereta. Recognised by Rome and protected by Italian carabinieri sealing the border, they forced the Committee of Freedom government to surrender. Federico Bigi, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs ever since, embodies their legacy.

They regard San Marino as a Western outpost that must never again fall to a popular front, and would set aside ordinary politics to keep the communists out. They rely on Italy's Christian Democrats, the American embassy and the Sammarinese emigrants of Detroit and New York, hundreds of whom were flown home to vote in 1969.

1.name: Partito Democratico Cristiano Sammarinese
1.text:
The Sammarinese Christian Democratic Party, founded in 1948, has led every government since the crisis of 1957 in partnership with the Independent Social Democrats, under the banner of the Popular Alliance. In the election of September 1969 it won 44 percent and 27 of the 60 seats in the Grand and General Council. Federico Bigi directs foreign policy, and Giancarlo Ghironzi serves as one of the two Captains Regent.

The party stands for Catholic social values, close friendship with Italy and firm anti-communism within the Western camp. Its base lies in the parishes, the farming families of the castelli, the Catholic trade unionists of the CDLS and the emigrants abroad. Its leverage rests on patronage over public jobs, citizenship and licences, and on the revenues from stamps, coins and tourism.

2.name: Movimento per le Libertà Statutarie
2.text:
The Movement for Constitutional Freedoms was launched in 1964 by Leo Dominicini and Renzo Bonelli as a small liberal and radical alternative to the two great blocs of Sammarinese politics. It won a seat in the Grand and General Council in 1964 and held it in September 1969 with about two percent of the vote, sitting in opposition to the Christian Democratic coalition.

Inspired by Italy's Radical Party, it campaigns for civil liberties, a written declaration of citizens' rights, stronger checks on the power of the Council and the use of referendums. It favours a secular state and stands firmly in the Western camp. Its supporters are lawyers, teachers and professionals, and its leverage lies in its potential role as a hinge between the Christian Democrats and the Socialists.

3.name: Partito Socialista Democratico Indipendente Sammarinese
3.text:
The Sammarinese Independent Democratic Socialist Party was founded on 14 April 1957, when Alvaro Casali, expelled as secretary of the Socialist Party for opposing its alliance with the Communists, led a breakaway group that merged with the small Social Democratic Party. Its defection toppled the left-wing government that year. Since then it has governed with the Christian Democrats, winning 18 percent in 1969, and Casali currently serves as Captain Regent.

The party combines democratic socialism with uncompromising anti-communism and looks to Giuseppe Saragat's Italian Democratic Socialists as its model. It defends social insurance, public works and workers' rights inside the Western alliance. Its base lies among civil servants, artisans and moderate workers, and its leverage comes from holding the balance of the governing majority.

4.name: Partito Comunista Sammarinese
4.text:
The Sammarinese Communist Party governed the republic together with the Socialists in the Committee of Freedom from 1945 until the crisis of 1957, when defections cost the left its majority. Since then it has been in opposition, but it remains the second force in the country, winning 23 percent and 14 seats in September 1969 under veteran leaders such as Ermenegildo Gasperoni.

The party follows the line of the Italian Communist Party, combining loyalty to the Soviet Union with a parliamentary road to socialism. It demands public control of key services, a larger welfare state and greater independence from Italian tutelage. Its strength lies in the factories, among building workers and in the CSdL trade union confederation, and in the support of its powerful Italian comrades across the border.

5.name: La Contestazione del Titano
5.text:
The Titano Protest gathers the Sammarinese youth swept up in the revolt of 1968: students at the universities of Bologna and Urbino, apprentices and young workers who commute to the factories of Rimini. They took part in the occupations and assemblies of the Italian student movement and in the strikes of the Hot Autumn of 1969, and now argue in the cafés of Borgo Maggiore and Serravalle.

They scorn both the Christian Democratic establishment and the Communist Party, which they consider part of the system. Reading Il Manifesto and Lotta Continua, they call for workers' assemblies, solidarity with Vietnam and an end to the authority of priests, parties and fathers. Their leverage lies in their energy, their mastery of the assembly and the example of the Italian movement.

6.name: La Vecchia Guardia
6.text:
The Old Guard are the communist veterans who built the party in the anti-fascist underground of the 1930s and learned their politics in the years of Stalin. They distrust the parliamentary caution of the current leadership, the growing pull of Italian reformism and the long-haired generation of 1968 alike, and they hold firm positions in the party sections and the cooperatives.

They remain loyal to Moscow without reservation and bristle at the Italian Communist Party's open disapproval of the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968. Socially conservative and suspicious of student radicals, they see discipline, party unity and the Soviet example as the only guarantees against Christian Democratic hegemony. Their leverage lies in old networks within the party apparatus, the trade union and the cooperative movement.

7.name: Gli Eredi del Comitato
7.text:
The Heirs of the Committee are those on the left who still regard the Committee of Freedom government of 1945 to 1957 as the republic's legitimate order and the events of Rovereta as a coup staged by Italy. Embittered by the blockade imposed by Italian carabinieri and by twelve years of exclusion from power, they meet in the old party sections and workers' clubs.

They believe that a popular majority, once restored, must never again be dislodged: the left should rule through a strong executive, a people's militia and a purge of the Rovereta men, and break Italian tutelage by seeking recognition and trade in the socialist countries. Their leverage lies in the memory of 1957 and in disciplined militants ready to act if the left regains power.

8.name: Nehzat-e Azadi-ye Iran
8.text:
The Freedom Movement of Iran was founded in 1961 by Mehdi Bazargan, Ayatollah Mahmoud Taleghani and Yadollah Sahabi to unite Islamic faith with Mossadegh's constitutional nationalism. Banned by the Shah, with its leaders imprisoned for years after 1963, it survives through underground circles and through Iranian students abroad, including the many who study medicine and engineering at Bologna, Padua and Perugia, a short journey from San Marino.

The movement calls for a constitutional government accountable to the people and guided by Islamic ethics, an end to the Shah's dictatorship and to dependence on the United States, and social justice. It rejects both Marxism and clerical absolutism. In Italy its leverage is minimal, resting on student associations, prayer meetings and pamphlets smuggled home.

9.name: Hey'at-ha-ye Mo'talefe-ye Eslami
9.text:
The Islamic Coalition Societies were formed in 1963 by religious associations of the Tehran bazaar loyal to Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini. After Khomeini's exile in 1964, members of the network assassinated Prime Minister Hassan Ali Mansur in January 1965; four were executed and the rest driven underground. Khomeini now teaches in Najaf, and his declarations reach a handful of devout Iranian students in the Italian universities near San Marino.

The Coalition wants the Shah overthrown and a state governed by Islamic law under the guidance of the senior Shia clergy, free of American and Israeli influence. Austere and secretive, it is financed by bazaar merchants through religious dues. Abroad its influence is tiny, resting on leaflets, smuggled sermons and small prayer circles of students.

10.name: Centro Islamico Culturale d'Italia
10.text:
The Islamic Cultural Centre of Italy was founded in Rome in 1966 by the ambassadors of Muslim states accredited to Italy, with the Saudi embassy prominent among its patrons. It organises Friday prayers, religious instruction and assistance for the small Muslim population of Italy, made up of diplomats, students and traders, and hopes to obtain land for a great mosque in the capital.

The Centre represents conservative, state-sponsored Sunni Islam and avoids political radicalism. It treats loyalty to the host country and friendship with the Muslim monarchies as natural companions. For the few Muslims who pass through San Marino and the Romagna it is the nearest recognised religious authority. Its leverage lies in diplomatic backing and in the wealth of its Gulf and North African sponsors.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani and is banned throughout the Arab world for its attempts to win over army officers. Its ideas circulate among the Jordanian and Palestinian students who fill the University for Foreigners in Perugia and the faculties of Bologna, meeting in small study circles and passing its pamphlets among fellow Arabs.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and every existing Muslim regime, demanding a restored caliphate that would unite the Islamic world against both Western and Soviet power. It renounces armed action for now and concentrates on persuasion and on winning influential supporters. Around San Marino its leverage is negligible, but its cadres are disciplined, patient and convinced that history is on their side.

12.name: Jama'at al-Ikhwan al-Muslimin
12.text:
The Muslim Brotherhood, founded in Egypt in 1928 by Hassan al-Banna, is suppressed by Nasser's regime and persecuted by the Ba'athists in Syria, but its exiles have built a European base at the Islamic Centre of Geneva directed by Said Ramadan. In Italy its sympathisers are Syrian, Jordanian and Palestinian students at Perugia, Bologna and Padua, who organise prayers, study circles and the first Islamic student associations.

The Brotherhood presents Islam as a complete system of faith, law and social order and seeks to Islamise society gradually through preaching, education and charity. It is hostile to Arab socialism and communism alike. Near San Marino its presence is limited to students and visitors, and its leverage lies in its international network and its organisational discipline.

13.name: Consiglio dei XII
13.text:
The Council of Twelve is one of the oldest institutions of the republic: twelve members elected by the Grand and General Council at the start of each legislature and presided over by the Captains Regent. It acts as an administrative body and as the highest court of appeal, authorises the purchase of land by foreigners and oversees guardianships and many questions of property and citizenship.

Its members, drawn from the leading families and the governing parties, embody a paternalist tradition that places order, continuity and the authority of the institutions above party quarrels and Cold War alignments. Should politics break down, they would govern as a council of notables. Their leverage lies in their control of land, property disputes and the countless permits on which Sammarinese life depends.

14.name: Azione Cattolica
14.text:
Catholic Action is the organised lay apostolate of the Church in San Marino, which belongs to the Diocese of Montefeltro, whose bishop resides across the border at Pennabilli. Through its men's, women's and youth branches it runs catechism, recreation centres and charitable works in the parishes of the castelli, and it has trained many of the Christian Democrats who now govern the republic.

Its members defend the Catholic family, religious education and public morality against secularism, divorce and the permissive culture spreading from the Riviera. Wary of the Cold War partisanship of politicians, they see the faith rather than any foreign alliance as the foundation of Sammarinese liberty. Their leverage lies in the parish network, the authority of the clergy and the votes of devout women and rural families.

15.name: Cassa di Risparmio della Repubblica di San Marino
15.english: Savings Bank of the Republic of San Marino
15.native_full: Cassa di Risparmio della Repubblica di San Marino
15.text:
The Savings Bank of the Republic of San Marino, founded in 1882, is the largest financial institution of the republic and the treasury of its leading families, foundations and public bodies. Together with the Banca Agricola Commerciale and a few smaller credit houses, it gathers the remittances of emigrants, the profits of the tourist boom and a growing flow of deposits from across the Italian border.

The banking and propertied elite favours low taxes, light regulation and political stability above all. It works comfortably with the Christian Democrats but fears both communist nationalisation and Italian pressure on the republic's financial autonomy. Its leverage lies in credit for construction, industry and tourism, and in the quiet influence of its directors on the men who govern.

16.name: Associazione Nazionale dell'Industria Sammarinese
16.text:
The National Association of Sammarinese Industry was founded in 1945 to represent the republic's manufacturers. Its members range from ceramics, textile and furniture workshops to the new factories that sprang up in the 1960s to take advantage of low taxes, cheap land and easy access to the Italian market, transforming an agricultural republic into an industrial one.

The association champions free enterprise, low taxation, light regulation and labour peace, and resists both union demands and state intervention. It defends the republic's fiscal sovereignty as its chief competitive advantage. Its leverage lies in jobs and investment: every new plant strengthens its voice with the government, while its members' prosperity depends on preserving San Marino's distinct status from Italy.

17.name: Salviamo il Titano
17.text:
Save the Titano is a loose circle of teachers, artists, local historians and old families alarmed by the building boom on the slopes of Monte Titano. Since the opening of the cable car in 1959 and the arrival of mass tourism from the Adriatic beaches, hotels, souvenir shops, car parks and new housing have spread from the City of San Marino to Borgo Maggiore and the valleys below.

They call for strict planning laws, protection of the medieval towers and walls, limits on traffic and quarrying and preservation of the farmland of the castelli. Standing above parties and blocs, they see the landscape as part of the republic's identity and its claim to survival. Their leverage is moral and cultural, resting on the local press and the prestige of scholars.

18.name: Partito Socialista Sammarinese
18.text:
The Sammarinese Socialist Party, founded in 1892, is the oldest party of the republic and led the struggle that restored the Arengo and an elected Grand and General Council in 1906. Allied with the Communists in the Committee of Freedom, it governed from 1945 until the split of its moderate wing brought down the government in 1957. In September 1969 it won 12 percent and 7 seats and remains in opposition.

The party stands for democratic socialism, workers' rights, secular education and neutrality between the blocs, in close contact with the Italian Socialist Party. Torn between its old alliance with the Communists and the temptation of government with the Christian Democrats, it holds the balance of the left. Its base lies among workers, artisans and the CSdL trade union.

19.name: Partito Comunista (marxista-leninista) di San Marino
19.text:
The Communist Party (Marxist–Leninist) of San Marino grew out of the Marxist–Leninist Movement founded in March 1968 by dissidents of the Sammarinese Communist Party under Giuseppe Fabbri, a former Communist member of the Grand and General Council. In September 1969 it became the first list in the republic's history to win no seat, polling 161 votes.

It denounces the Communist Party as revisionist and the Soviet Union as social-imperialist, takes its line from Mao Zedong's China and Enver Hoxha's Albania, and acts as a fraternal party of the Communist Party of Italy (Marxist–Leninist). It calls for revolutionary class struggle and rejects parliamentary compromise. Its leverage is tiny, resting on a handful of militants, wall posters and the Peking Review.

20.name: Il Titano ai Sammarinesi
20.text:
The Titano for the Sammarinese voices the resentment of shopkeepers, small farmers and returning emigrants who feel that their republic is treated as a province of Italy. They recall the closing of the casino under Italian pressure in the early 1950s, the blockade of 1957 and the conventions that restrict the republic's own coinage, broadcasting and customs, and they complain of Italian speculators buying up land.

The movement demands the renegotiation of the treaties with Italy, a casino, a Sammarinese coinage and broadcasting service, and preference for citizens in jobs and property. It distrusts all the established parties as clients of Rome. Its leverage lies in local pride, emigrant networks and the frustration of voters who see the republic's sovereignty eroded year by year.

21.name: La Fiamma del Titano
21.text:
The Titano Flame gathers the unrepentant survivors of the Sammarinese Fascist Party, which ruled the republic from 1923 until the fall of Mussolini in 1943, and a few young men drawn to the Italian Social Movement across the border. Fascism ended in San Marino amid the bombing of 1944 and the arrival of the Allies, but its veterans still meet privately in the castelli.

They admire Giorgio Almirante, who became leader of the Italian Social Movement in 1969, and call for a strong state, the suppression of communism and a corporative order rooted in Catholic and national tradition. Hostile to both superpowers in rhetoric, they are anti-communist in practice. Their leverage is minimal, resting on old loyalties and contacts with the far right of the Romagna.

22.name: Guardia di Rocca
22.text:
The Guard of the Rock is the professional core of San Marino's small military corps, which also include the ceremonial Guard of the Council, the Uniformed Militia drawn from citizen reservists and the Gendarmerie. Its soldiers in green and red uniforms guard the Palazzo Pubblico and the Captains Regent, watch the frontier and perform the republic's ceremonies, under officers from old Sammarinese families.

The corps are loyal to the institutions and lack real fighting power, but they remain the only armed force of the state and remember the crisis of 1957, when order hung on armed volunteers and Italian carabinieri. In a breakdown of civil authority their commanders could assume emergency powers. Their leverage lies in the monopoly of arms on the mountain and in public respect for tradition.

23.name: Diocesi di Montefeltro
23.text:
The Diocese of Montefeltro, whose bishop resides at Pennabilli in Italy, embraces San Marino and keeps alive the cult of Saint Marinus, the stonemason who according to tradition founded the republic in 301. The Church presides over every civic ritual, from the installation of the Captains Regent each April and October to the feast of the patron saint, and the great majority of Sammarinese are practising Catholics.

The clergy stands above the parties as guardian of the ancient statutes, the family and Christian morality, and many traditionalists would welcome a confessional order in which the bishop arbitrates public life. The diocese's leverage lies in the pulpit, the parish network, Catholic Action and the Christian Democrats' dependence on Catholic votes.
